shifts-movements-s1.title: Marlow Street Bakery's busy week
shifts-movements-s1.text: Marlow Street Bakery keeps a graph of its croissant market: price per croissant on the vertical axis, croissants sold per day on the horizontal axis, a downward curve D for its customers and an upward curve S for what it offers. During one week: on Monday the bakery cuts the price of a croissant from \$4 to \$3. On Tuesday a large office opens next door. On Thursday the butter the bakery buys doubles in price. On Friday a cafe across the street starts selling its own croissants for \$2. (An invented bakery.)

items.q: On a graph with price on the vertical axis, which change causes a movement along a curve rather than a shift of it?
options: A change in the number of buyers
A change in buyers' incomes
A change in the price of the good itself
A change in the cost of the sellers' materials

why.correct: Only a change in a variable on one of the axes moves the market along the curve. The good's own price is on the vertical axis.
options: The number of buyers is not on an axis, so a change in it shifts the curve.
Income is not on an axis, so a change in it shifts the curve.
Right: price is on an axis, so the market moves along the curve.
Material costs are not on an axis, so a change in them shifts the sellers' curve.

items.q: A curve "shifts right" on a graph with quantity across and price up. What does that mean?
options: At every price, the quantity is larger than before
At each quantity, the price is lower than before
The price rose and the quantity rose along the same curve
The curve became steeper

why.correct: A shift right moves every point of the curve to a larger quantity at the same price.
options: Right: each price now goes with a larger quantity.
This reads the move up and down; "right" is about quantity at each price.
Moving along one curve is a movement, not a shift.
A shift moves the curve; it does not have to change how steep it is.

items.q: A new apartment building opens and at every price more people want to buy sandwiches at a deli. Shift the right curve the right way.

why.correct: More sandwiches wanted at every price is a shift of the buyers' curve D to the right. The sandwich price did not cause it, so it is not a movement along D.

slips.S: The new building brings buyers, so it moves the buyers' curve D; a change in the deli's own costs would move S.

items.q: The flour a bakery buys becomes more expensive, so at every price the bakery offers fewer loaves. Shift the right curve the right way.

why.correct: Fewer loaves offered at every price is a shift of the sellers' curve S to the left.

key.because: a rise in the cost of flour

slips.D: Flour is a cost for the bakery, so it moves the sellers' curve S, not the buyers' curve D.

items.q: A furniture maker buys a new saw that cuts twice as fast, so at every price it can offer more chairs. Shift the right curve the right way.

why.correct: A faster saw lowers the cost of each chair, so more chairs are offered at every price: S shifts right.

key.because: a faster saw that lowers costs

slips.D: The saw changes what the maker can offer, so it moves S; buyers want the same number of chairs as before at each price.

items.q: The price of movie tickets rises and nothing else changes. Place point X where buyers end up on the curve D.

why.correct: A higher price, the variable on the vertical axis, moves buyers up along D to a smaller quantity. The curve itself stays where it is.

items.q: A student says, "The price of bus fares fell, so the curve D for bus rides shifted right." What is wrong with the claim?
options: A lower fare shifts D left, not right
The fare is on the horizontal axis, so D stays put
Nothing is wrong: a lower fare shifts D right
A fare change is a movement along D, not a shift

why.correct: The fare is the price on the vertical axis. A lower fare moves riders down along the same curve to more rides.
options: A price change does not shift D in either direction.
Price is on the vertical axis of a market graph, not the horizontal one.
A price change is a movement, not a shift.
Right: a price change is a movement along the curve.

items.q: On Monday the bakery cuts the price of a croissant from \$4 to \$3. How does its graph show this?
options: A shift of D to the right, at each price
A movement down along D
A shift of D to the left, at each price
A movement up along D to a smaller quantity

why.correct: The price is on the vertical axis, so a lower price moves buyers down along D to more croissants sold.
options: The price change does not shift D; it moves buyers along it.
Right: same curve, new point.
Nothing about buyers changed except the price, so D stays put.
A LOWER price moves buyers down along D, to a larger quantity.

items.q: On Tuesday a large office opens next door. How does the graph show this?
options: A movement down along D, as after a price cut
D shifts right: more are wanted at each price
S shifts right: the bakery offers more at each price
D shifts left: fewer croissants are wanted at each price

why.correct: More nearby customers want more croissants at every price. That change is not on either axis, so D shifts right.
options: The price did not change, so this is not a movement along D.
Right: more buyers shift D right.
The office brings buyers, not cheaper baking, so S stays put.
More buyers raise the quantity wanted at each price, so D moves right, not left.

items.q: On Thursday the butter the bakery buys doubles in price. How does the graph show this?
options: D shifts left: buyers want fewer croissants
A movement up along S to a larger quantity
S shifts right: the bakery offers more croissants at each price
S shifts left: fewer croissants offered at each price

why.correct: Butter is a cost for the bakery. Higher costs mean fewer croissants offered at every price: S shifts left.
options: Buyers do not pay for the bakery's butter directly; the cost moves S, not D.
A movement along S needs a change in the croissant price itself.
Higher costs make the bakery offer fewer croissants, not more.
Right: a higher cost shifts S left.

items.q: On Friday a cafe across the street starts selling its own croissants for \$2. What is the most likely change on Marlow Street Bakery's graph?
options: D shifts left: some buyers go to the cafe
D shifts right: customers want more croissants
A movement down along the curve D
S shifts left: the bakery bakes fewer croissants

why.correct: A cheaper choice across the street pulls some buyers away, so fewer Marlow Street croissants are wanted at every price: D shifts left. Marlow Street's own price did not change.
options: Right: fewer buyers at every price.
The cafe pulls customers away, not toward the bakery.
Marlow Street's own price did not change, so this is not a movement along D.
The cafe does not change the bakery's costs; it changes what buyers want.

items.q: Make the explanation specific: a cafe raises the price of its muffins and sells fewer. Fill in each blank.

why.correct: A change in the variable on an axis is a movement along the curve; anything else shifts it.

specific.frame: The ___ changed, and it is the variable on ___, so the graph shows ___.

variable.label: What changed
options: price of muffins
number of buyers
cost of flour

why.1: Nothing in the scenario says the number of buyers changed; only the muffin price did.
why.2: The scenario changes the muffin price, not the cafe's costs.

axis.label: Which axis
options: the vertical axis
neither axis

why.1: Price is on the vertical axis of a market graph, so it is on an axis.

result.label: What the graph shows
options: a movement up along D
a shift of D to the left

why.1: A change in the good's own price never shifts D; buyers move along it to a smaller quantity.

specific.model: The price of muffins changed, and it is the variable on the vertical axis, so the graph shows a movement up along D to a smaller quantity, not a shift of the curve.

items.q: Put the steps for deciding between a shift and a movement in order.
options: Name what changed in the scenario
Check whether it is a variable on one of the axes
If it is, move along the curve; if not, shift the curve
For a shift, label the new curve 2 and draw an arrow

why.correct: Start from the cause, test it against the axes, decide shift or movement, then, for a shift, show it on the graph with labels.
